Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant), XXXX XXXX XXXX (Elder Minor Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXX (Younger Minor Appellant) are citizens of Nigeria and appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated February 8, 2019, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant), XXXX XXXX XXXX (Elder Minor Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXX (Younger Minor Appellant) are citizens of Nigeria and appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated February 8, 2019, rejecting their claims for refugee protection. The Appellants are requesting that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the RPD's negative determination and find that they are Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. In the alternative, the Appellants request the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted panel. The Appellants have requested to submit new evidence and have requested an oral hearing.

The Principal Appellant was appointed to be the designated representative (DR) of the minor Appellants at the RPD proceeding, and she continues to be the DR for the minor Appellants for the purposes of this appeal.1 DETERMINATION OF THE APPEAL

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

The Appellants allege that the Principal Appellant's husband's parents want the Elder Minor Appellant to undergo family rituals that involve incision marks, participating in sacrifices, dancing with masquerades and drinking concoctions. The Principal Appellant and her husband are Christians and refused his participation in the rituals. The husband's parents threatened to force him to undergo the rituals and threatened to kill the Appellants if they do not agree.

The husband reported his parents to police, but the police did not assist. The Appellants went into hiding but were located by the husband's family. The Appellants left Nigeria and arrived in Turkey on XXXX XXXX, 2018. They arrived in the United States on XXXX XXXX, 2018 and entered Canada XXXX XXXX, 2018.

The Appellants had a refugee determination hearing on November 16, 2018. In a written decision issued on February 8, 2019, the RPD rejected the claim. The RPD found the Appellants lacking in credibility.

The RAD applies a standard of correctness for questions of fact, mixed fact and law, and law. I may defer to the RPD in assessing findings involving the credibility of oral testimony if I find that it had a meaningful advantage in the circumstances.2 In this appeal, I find that the RPD did not have a meaningful advantage. ADMISSIBILITY OF EVIDENCE SUBMITTED ON APPEAL

The Appellants propose the following documents as new evidence: 1) an affidavit of the Principal Appellant's husband3 dated XXXX XXXX, 2019 and treasury receipts;4 and 2) a letter from police dated XXXX XXXX, 2019.5 According to subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, new evidence will only be admitted where the evidence (1) arose after the rejection of the claim, (2) was not reasonably available, or (3) could not reasonably have been expected to have been presented in the circumstances at the time of the rejection.6 Appellants are to make full and detailed submissions in their memorandum regarding how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) and how that evidence relates to the appellants.7

If one of the factors of subsection 110(4) is met, the RAD will proceed to consider the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh,8 namely if the evidence is credible, relevant and new.9 The affidavit of the Principal Appellant's husband is accepted into evidence

The Appellants submit that the affidavit of the Principal Appellant's husband submitted on appeal (husband's second affidavit) meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) because it arose reasonably after the hearing and the Appellants did not anticipate that the RPD would disbelieve the Appellants regarding the husband and the absence of any direct threats to his life. They also argue that the affidavit is relevant as it contradicts the RPD finding that there is and was no direct threat to his life in the hands of his parents and confirms that the husband's parents are still interested in the Appellants. They argue that the affidavit is credible as it is a sworn document from Nigeria.

I find that the affidavit of the Principal Appellant's husband meets subsection 110(4). The affidavit addresses an inconsistency that the RPD Member found in the husband's affidavit that was submitted to the RPD (husband's first affidavit) regarding whether the husband was threatened. The husband's second affidavit also addresses the RPD finding that the husband's parents were aware that the husband reported them to police. As these issues were not raised at the RPD hearing, I accept that the Appellants could not reasonably have been expected to provide this information prior to reviewing the RPD reasons.
The husband's second affidavit also refers to the continued interest of the husband's parents in the Appellants, which are events that arose after rejection of the claim.

I find the husband's second affidavit meets the Singh/Raza factors. The affidavit is a sworn document and meets the credibility factor for purposes of admissibility. The information contained in the affidavit is relevant as it addresses credibility findings of the RPD and the husband's parents' continued interest in the Appellants. Finally, as outlined above, the information contained in the affidavit is new. As a result of the foregoing, the husband's second affidavit is accepted into evidence. The letter from police is not accepted into evidence

The Appellants submit that the letter from police is dated after the rejection and arose reasonably after the decision was made and the Appellants did not anticipate that the RPD would disbelieve the validity of the police report. The Appellants submit that the letter from police is credible as it emanates from a government institution in Nigeria and bears the presumption of authenticity. The Appellants submit that the letter from police is relevant because it speaks directly to why the RPD concluded that the police report was fraudulent.

I find that the letter from police meets subsection 110(4) as it contradicts findings of fact made by the RPD which were not raised at the hearing. I accept that the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected to have presented it at the time of the rejection.

With regard to the Singh/Raza credibility factor, the RPD found that the police report was fraudulent on the basis of a spelling error in the report. The letter from police addresses the spelling error and authenticity of the report. In order to assess the credibility of the letter from police for purposes of admissibility, I first need to assess the police report. The RAD finds that the police report is fraudulent

The RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that the police report submitted by the Appellants was fraudulent on the basis that it contains two different spellings for the police station address. The RPD assigned no weight to the police report considering the spelling error and the availability and prevalence of fraudulent documents in Nigeria.

The Appellants submit that spelling errors on the face of a document do not render it invalid and that it is an error to focus on superficial errors in grammar and spelling to discredit evidentiary documents. The Appellants submit that the police report emanated from a government institution and therefore is presumed authentic. The Appellants submit that fraudulent documents being widely available in a country do not mean that every document from that country is fraudulent.

While I accept the Appellants' argument that the RPD erred in its means of assessing the police report, after my independent assessment, I find that the RPD was correct in concluding that, on a balance of probabilities, the police report is fraudulent.

I agree that it is an error to focus solely on superficial errors in grammar and spelling to discredit evidentiary documents. The police report letterhead refers to its address as "XXXX XXXX" whereas the address portion at the bottom of the report refers to the address as "XXXX XXXX." The RPD found the police report fraudulent "given this is an alleged report from an official police source that misstates its own address."10 While I agree with the RPD finding that the misspelling undermines the credibility of the police report, this cannot be the sole reason upon which to conclude that it is fraudulent.

However, there are also other issues with the police report. The content of the police report is inconsistent with the documentary evidence. The police report states the husband "...informed the officer of how his parent wanted to initiate his son into a cult and make him go through baebaric rituals that could scar him and even result to death. But being a family matter, an issue between father and son, he was asked to go home and try to make peace amicably."11 As indicated above, the Appellants state that the husband's parents want the Elder Minor Appellant to go through initiation rituals, including making incisions on different parts of his body. The Appellants have provided documentary evidence with respect to initiations, scarification and tribal markings.

The documentary evidence indicates that Nigeria's 2003 Child Rights Act declares the practice of tribal markings on children illegal in Nigeria and can result in a monetary fine or prison term of up to a month, or both.12 The documentary evidence also indicates that both Osun, the state where the husband's parents reside, and Lagos, the state where the Appellants resided and in which they filed the police report, have passed the Child Rights Act into law.13 The documentary evidence states that parents can obtain protection from police if they have family members who want to apply tribal markings on their child and that "there is not very much trouble enforcing the law, even in rural parts of the country."14 I find the police report and other evidence indicating that the police would not assist inconsistent with the documentary evidence. I note that this inconsistency was not put to the Appellants, however, the Federal Court has stated that the RPD is not required to confront a claimant with contradictions between the Appellant's documents and the material provided in the National Documentation Package (NDP).15

I further note that the issuance of the police report is inconsistent with the documentary evidence. The documentary evidence states that police reports can only be obtained from the police station that recorded the complaint or incident.16 The police report and husband's first affidavit state he reported to the XXXX XXXX Division, Lagos State. However, the report was issued by the General Investigation SectionXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The report states that the case was later transferred to XXXX XXXX.

At the hearing, the RPD Member noted that the husband reported to police on XXXX 15, 2018, however, the police report was dated XXXX XXXX, 2018. The RPD Member asked the Principal Appellant why the husband did not get the report at the time that he made the report to which she responded that her husband had to go to XXXX to get the report because police reports from XXXX XXXX are not recognized internationally.17 However, this is inconsistent with the documentary evidence which states that police reports can only be obtained from the police station at which the incident was recorded. I find that this further undermines the authenticity of the police report.

While I agree that government documents are presumed authentic, I find this presumption is rebutted by the above-noted errors and inconsistencies with the documentary evidence regarding the content and issuance of the police report. Further, while I agree that fraudulent documents being widely available in a country does not mean that every document from that country is fraudulent, I do not rely solely on the prevalence of fraudulent documents to find the police report fraudulent. Rather, as noted above, there are other concerns with the police report.

As a result of the foregoing, and in light of the availability of fraudulent documents in Nigeria, I find on a balance of probabilities, that the police report is fraudulent. The letter from police is not accepted into evidence

The letter from police addresses the spelling errors in the police report and is from the same source as the police report, which has been found to be fraudulent. The Federal Court has stated that submitting a false or irregular document may have an impact on the weight assigned to other documents provided, especially where they are interrelated.18 I find that the fraudulent police report diminishes the credibility of the letter from police. Further, I note that the letter from police also appears to contain a spelling error in the address portion of the document. The address reads "Crimal Investigation Department Annex." It appears that this should read "Criminal."

As a result of the foregoing, I find the letter from police not credible for purposes of admissibility. Therefore, the letter from police is not accepted into evidence. The request for an oral hearing is denied

The RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in subsection 110(3) of the IRPA that (1) raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal, (2) is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim and, (3) if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.19

I find that the husband's second affidavit meets the first two requirements of subsection 110(6). However, I find it does not meet the third requirement because, if accepted, it would not justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim. The affidavit does not overcome the credibility findings. Further, I am able to assess the affidavit based on its content without holding a hearing, therefore I choose not to hold a hearing on this evidence. General credibility impugned due to submission of fraudulent police report

The Federal Court has stated that submitting a false or irregular document may have an impact on the overall credibility of an Appellant.20 I find that the Principal Appellant has undermined her credibility by providing a fraudulent police report in support of the claim.
The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in its credibility assessment and assessment of the Appellants' documentary evidence. ANALYSIS The RPD did not err in finding the Appellants' claim implausible

The RPD found it implausible that the husband, who took the lead in refusing to allow his family to perform the rituals on the Elder Minor Appellant, remained in Nigeria, while the Appellants fled for their safety. The RPD found that, if the husband's family was so unyielding, adamant and insistent that the rituals be carried out, it was implausible that they would let him off the hook, even after he reported them to police.

The Appellants submit that the RPD assumed and wrongfully concluded that since the lives of the Appellants were threatened, by implication, the life of the husband had to be threatened. The Appellants submit that the explanation provided by the Principal Appellant and in the husband's affidavit that he was not directly threatened is reasonable. The Appellants submit that there is no evidence that the husband's family were aware of the report to police and the RPD wrongfully inferred that the report to police should have exposed the husband to the ire of his family. The Appellants submit that the RPD relied on Canadian paradigms when assessing the Appellants' claim and that implausibility findings should only be made in the clearest of cases.
Although I accept some of the Appellants' arguments, I find that the RPD was correct in finding the claim implausible.

I reject the Appellants' argument that the RPD wrongfully concluded that, since the lives of the Appellants were threatened, by implication, the life of the husband had to be threatened. I concur with the RPD finding that it is implausible that the Appellants had to flee Nigeria for their safety due to the husband's family's unyielding insistence that the Elder Minor Appellant undergo the rituals, while the husband remained safely in Nigeria.

As noted by the RPD Member, it is entitled to make reasonable findings based on implausibilities, common sense and rationality. While I agree that implausibility findings should only be made in the clearest of cases, I find that this is such a case.

I accept the Appellants' argument that the RPD erred in finding that the husband's family was aware that he reported them to police. I find that the evidence does not support this finding. However, I find that the alleged situation remains implausible even without the husband's family knowing that he reported them to police.

The husband's second affidavit provides information on why he believes he was not initially threatened by his parents. His affidavit states he believes it was because his parents thought that he would come around as he is their son and he understood the Yoruba customs and traditions. I find this to be inconsistent with the Appellants' Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative which states that when the husband's parents raised the issue of rituals with the Principal Appellant and her husband, the husband asked them why they were only hearing of it at that time, suggesting that he was unaware of the customary expectation.

I find that the credibility of the husband's second affidavit is diminished by the provision of the fraudulent police report. The Federal Court has stated that submitting a false or irregular document may have an impact on the weight assigned to other documents provided, especially when they are interrelated.21 I find the husband's affidavit interrelated to the police report as they both relate to the husband's parents wanting the Elder Minor Appellant to undergo rituals. Furthermore, the husband was the person who allegedly filed the police report. As a result, I assign no weight to the husband's second affidavit and do not accept his explanation as to why he believes he was not threatened by his parents.

I reject the Appellants' argument that the RPD relied on Canadian paradigms when assessing the Appellants' claim. I do not see, nor do the Appellants explain, how the RPD did so. Rule 3(3)(g) of the RAD Rules requires that Appellants provide full and detailed submissions regarding the errors that are the grounds of the appeal and where the errors are located.22 As stated by the Federal Court, Appellants cannot simply raise an issue and expect the RAD to find evidence to support it.23 Without more explanation of how the RPD relied on Canadian paradigms, I find this argument without merit. The evidence is inconsistent regarding whether the husband was threatened

The RPD found the husband's first affidavit inconsistent in that it states he remained in Nigeria because he was not directly threatened by his family yet later states he had been threatened repeatedly if he did not ensure the Appellants return to Nigeria.

The Appellants submit that the husband's first affidavit states it was after the Appellants left Nigeria that his family started to ask for the Appellants and, although it stated there would be dire consequences, that did not convey that the husband's life had been threatened. The Appellants submit that the RPD misapprehended the evidence.

I accept the Appellants' argument that the RPD erred in finding that there was an inconsistency in the husband's first affidavit. However, as explained below, I find that there was an inconsistency between the Principal Appellant's testimony and husband's first affidavit regarding whether the husband was threatened.

I have reviewed the record as part of my independent assessment. The husband's first affidavit states: I stayed back because my life wasn't threatened directly at the time by my family. After my wife and kids arrived Canada in XXXX 2018, my parents came to my house asking me to have my wife and kids return home, so my son can undergo the rituals. They call me almost every other day telling me to bring my son and wife back home. My father has visited me on four different occasions threatening that there will be dire consequences if I refused to bring them back to Nigeria. They are still very persistent insisting my wife comes back home with XXXX XXXX.24

I find that the RPD erred in its finding that the husband's first affidavit was inconsistent. The way the first affidavit reads, the husband was not threatened prior to the Appellants leaving Nigeria, but was threatened after they left.

However, this raises an inconsistency between the husband's second affidavit and the Principal Appellant's testimony. The RPD Member notes that the husband's first affidavit states his life was not directly threatened and asked the Principal Appellant if her husband had been "threatened at all by his parents," to which she responded "no, not that she knows of."25 The Principal Appellant's testimony that her husband was not threatened by his family is inconsistent with the husband's affidavit, which indicates that his father visited him four times and threatened dire consequences if he refused to bring the Elder Minor Appellant back to Nigeria.

The husband's second affidavit states: "That I never said that my life was threatened, I stated in the previous affidavit that my father threatened that there will be dire consequences if my son does not return to Nigeria to carry out the ritual. He did not further explain the consequences or on whose head these consequences will fall on."26 I reject this explanation. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the threat of dire consequences if the husband refused to bring the Appellants back to Nigeria constitutes a threat to the husband, particularly in light of the fact that the Appellants are not in Nigeria. As a result, I find that there is an inconsistency between the Principal Appellant's testimony and the husband's first affidavit regarding whether he was threatened by his parents.

I note that the Principal Appellant was not confronted with this inconsistency at the hearing. However, having regard to the factors set out by the Federal Court in Ngongo,27 I find that, in the circumstances, it was not necessary to confront the Principal Appellant. The inconsistency between the Principal Appellant's testimony and her husband's affidavit was obvious and in answer to a direct question from the RPD Member. The inconsistency was an actual contradiction in that, according to the Principal Appellant's testimony, her husband was not threatened, whereas according to the husband's affidavit, he was. The Appellants were on notice that credibility was an issue and were represented by counsel, who could have questioned her regarding the inconsistency. Although the Principal Appellant was communicating through an interpreter, no issue was raised regarding interpretation. Finally, the RPD decision was not based on this single inconsistency, but rather on a number of credibility concerns. I draw an adverse inference with respect to the Appellant's credibility as a result of this inconsistency. The RPD erred in finding the Appellants' failure to claim asylum in Turkey and the United States indicative of a lack of subjective fear
The RPD found the Appellants' failure to claim asylum in Turkey and the United States indicative of a lack of subjective fear, particularly in light of their previous travel to the United States.

The Appellants submit that delay in claiming may be a valid factor, but does not automatically result in a finding of a lack of subjective fear and that the circumstances and potential explanations for the delay must be considered. The Appellants submit that they provided a reasonable explanation for not claiming in Turkey and the United States. The Appellants submit that the RPD relied on the Appellants' previous travel to the United States to impeach their credibility.

While the Appellants' failure to claim in Turkey and the United States may initially appear indicative of a lack of subjective fear, I find that, upon consideration of their circumstances and explanation, their subjective fear is not undermined.

The Appellants were in Turkey for less than a week on their way to the United States. The Principal Appellant indicated that she stayed in Turkey for that time because she was travelling alone with the minor appellants, who were very young. The Principal Appellant indicated that she did not claim asylum in Turkey because she did not speak the language.

The Appellants were in the United States for one week prior to travelling to Canada. They had valid United States visitors' visas. The Principal Appellant's evidence was that she did not claim asylum in the United States for a number of reasons, one of which was the immigration policies at the time.

Considering the short time that the Appellants spent in Turkey and the United States and their explanations for not claiming, I find that their failure to claim does not undermine their subjective fear. The RPD erred in its assessment of the documentary evidence

The RPD assigned the husband's first affidavit little weight because of the implausibility that the family would let the husband off the hook in light of their insistence that the Elder Minor Appellant undergo the rituals. The RPD assigned the affidavits of the Principal Appellant's father and husband's aunt little weight because they corroborate an allegation that he found inherently not credible. The RPD also refers to confirmatory evidence of family members that is not subject to cross-examination as not being highly probative or credible evidence because it does not come from independent sources.

The Appellants refer to Federal Court jurisprudence that evidence must be considered in its entirety before making a finding of negative credibility against a claimant. The Appellants submit that the RPD arrived at a global credibility finding and gave no weight to the supporting documents in respect of the Appellants' claim. The Appellants submit that the courts have said that documents from family members should not be viewed as self-serving and that it is an error for the RPD to reject evidence from relatives on the sole basis that it is self-serving.

I accept the Appellant's argument that the RPD erred in its assessment of the documentary evidence by not considering the evidence in its entirety before making a credibility assessment. It is not clear from the reasons whether the RPD Member made a global credibility finding. In the absence of such a finding, I find that the RPD erred in using its credibility findings to discount the affidavits. The documentary evidence does not overcome the credibility concerns I have reviewed the documentary evidence as part of my independent assessment and find that the corroborating documents fail to overcome the credibility concerns. The husband's first affidavit28

The husband's first affidavit refers to the problems that he and the Appellants experienced with his family prior to and after leaving Nigeria. The affidavit indicates that, after the Appellants left, his parents continued to call him to inquire about the Appellants and that they threatened dire consequences if the husband did not bring the Elder Minor Appellant back to Nigeria. I find the husband's affidavit probative of whether the Appellants are at risk at the hands of the husband's family and their continued interest in the Appellants.

However, I find the husband's first affidavit not credible. As indicated above, the fraudulent police report diminishes the credibility of the affidavit. These documents are interrelated as both refer to the allegations that the husband's parents are trying to impose rituals on the Elder Minor Appellant. Further, the husband was the person who allegedly obtained the police report. In addition, as discussed above, the husband's affidavit is inconsistent with the Principal Appellant's testimony regarding whether he was threatened by his parents. As a result of the foregoing, I assign no weight to the husband's first affidavit. The husband's second affidavit29

The husband's second affidavit is addressed in the sections above. The husband's second affidavit addresses some of the findings of the RPD, namely an alleged inconsistency in the first affidavit regarding whether the husband was threatened, provides reasons why he believes he was not threatened, states that his parents were unaware that he reported to police and refers to the parents' continued interest in the Appellants. Although I find the content of the second affidavit probative, it is interrelated with the fraudulent police report, as it relates to the same underlying allegations of threats by the husband's parents and the husband was the person who allegedly obtained the police report. As a result, I assign no weight to the husband's second affidavit. The affidavit of the Principal Appellant's father30

There do not appear to be credibility concerns regarding the affidavit of the Principal Appellant's father. The content of the affidavit is probative. A large part of the affidavit recounts information that was not directly observed by the author but rather was relayed to him by the Principal Appellant. I assign little weight to this portion of the affidavit. The portion of the affidavit that the father appears to have direct knowledge of relates to the Appellants hiding at his home and the father receiving a phone call from the husband's family. I assign this portion of the affidavit some weight. The affidavit of the husband's aunt31

There do not appear to be credibility concerns regarding the affidavit of the husband's aunt. The majority of the affidavit of the husband's aunt refers to what happened to the husband's parent's first child (the husband's brother) after he performed the rituals. I find this information somewhat probative to whether the Appellants are at risk at the hand of the husband's parents and I assign some weight to this portion of the affidavit. The affidavit also refers to the husband advising the aunt that his family wanted his son to undergo the rituals. As this information was not directly observed by the husband's aunt and was relayed to her by the husband, I assign it little weight.

After my review of all of the documentary evidence, I find it fails to overcome the other credibility concerns, namely the provision of a fraudulent police report, the implausibility of the Appellants' claim and the inconsistency in the evidence regarding whether the husband was threatened by his parents. There is no basis for the claim of the Youngest Minor Appellant under section 96 or 97

The RPD found that, as it heard no evidence with respect to the Younger Minor Appellant's claim for protection in the United States, one of his countries of citizenship, except for the Principal Appellant's desire to be with her son, there was no basis for his claim for protection under either section 96 or 97 of the IRPA.
The Appellants submit that the RPD failed to consider the Principal Appellant's claim that the Youngest Minor Appellant would be exposed to trauma if he were returned to the United States.

While I agree that the RPD Member failed to specifically consider the emotional trauma that could result if the Principal Appellant was separated from the Younger Minor Appellant, the RPD and the RAD have no jurisdiction under the legislation to grant refugee protection on the basis of humanitarian and compassionate considerations. Rather, the role of the RPD and the RAD, is to determine whether there is a serious possibility of persecution for a claimant or whether, on a balance of probabilities, a claimant would be subject to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or to a danger of torture if the claimant were to return to his or her country of citizenship. I find the emotional trauma that the Youngest Minor Appellant may experience if he were to return to the United States does not meet these requirements.

For the foregoing reasons, I find that the RPD did not err in rejecting the Appellants' claim. While I find that some of the RPD's findings are in error, I find that the Appellants failed to provide credible evidence to support their allegations on a balance of probabilities.

I find that, as a result of the provision of a fraudulent police report, the implausibility of the claim and the inconsistency in the evidence regarding whether the husband was threatened, the Appellants have not established, on a balance of probabilities, the allegations that form the basis of their claim. I find that the provision of a fraudulent summons diminishes the Appellants' credibility and the credibility of documents submitted by the Appellants. Further, I find that the risk raised by the Younger Minor Appellant does not meet the requirements of section 96 or 97.

As a result, I find that the Appellants have not established that they face more than a mere possibility of persecution pursuant to section 96, or that they face harm, on a balance of probabilities pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.
